Campaign 1

Awareness campaign to provide electricity to two million people in Cameroon

A nationwide campaign to win the trust of households and bring them on board with a programme connecting two million people to electricity.

Funded by
World Bank
Amount
US$25 million (revolving fund)
Country
Cameroon
Period
2022–2025

  1. Communication challenge

    Persuading households to sign up to the initiative at a time of widespread mistrust of government-led development programmes and a loss of confidence in the authorities.

  2. Objectives

    Provide electricity to two million people in Cameroon.

  3. Target audiences

    Households in rural, semi-urban and urban areas.

  4. My role

    Senior Campaign Manager.

  5. Strategic approach

    The campaign began with a pilot phase built around a strong gender focus, and was then rolled out on a large scale.

  6. Creative concept

    The concept rests on a simple promise: “A household, an electric meter.” The goal was to make electricity feel concrete and within reach, not like a distant government project. In line with the gender focus of the pilot phase, women were the main voice of the campaign. The message was designed to spread the way news spreads in a neighbourhood: from one person to the next, in everyday language and with a touch of humour (“C’est le JAPAP de l’année !”). To overcome mistrust, the campaign put transparency first, showing who backs the programme, how repayments are tracked, who checks the work and where to complain. Every message ended with the same call to action: call the free number 8566 or register online.

  7. Channels used

    • Social media (Facebook)
    • WhatsApp community groups
    • Radio, including community radio
    • Television
    • Door-to-door and street outreach

  8. Dissemination approach

    We started in the pilot cities, then extended the campaign to the 687 localities covered by PERACE. On Facebook, I created and managed campaigns combining regular posts with paid ads aimed at households in the areas being connected. The same content was shared in WhatsApp groups and broadcast on television and on national and community radio. On the ground, our teams went door to door and out into the streets with flyers and leaflets, while billboards, banners and roll-ups kept the message visible in public places. Households could then sign up online or call 8566 with their questions or complaints.

  9. Measurable results

    More than 400,000 electrical connections were executed and around two million households were connected. On Facebook, 200,000 people reached by the campaign went on to contact the project.

Results at a glance

400,000+electrical connections executed
≈2 millionhouseholds connected
200,000people reached on Facebook who contacted the project

Campaign 2

Pilot awareness campaign on the dangers of moulds and aflatoxin

A one-month campaign across the ten regions of Cameroon to alert maize and sorghum producers, journalists and the public to a health and economic risk few people knew about.

Partners
IITA, IRAD and MINADER
Country
Cameroon, ten regions
Period
April 2017, one month
My title
Communication Campaign Manager

  1. Communication challenge

    Molds and aflatoxin cost Africa around US$670 million a year, according to the African Union, and are linked to 30% of deaths on the continent, with the highest rate in sub-Saharan Africa. Yet farmers and consumers knew almost nothing about the risk carried by poorly dried crops and by some everyday foods.

  2. Objectives

    Alert about 30,000 producers across the ten regions of Cameroon, together with the media, to the dangers of moulds and aflatoxin for human health and for the move to second-generation agriculture.

  3. Target audiences

    Directly: maize and sorghum producers. Indirectly: journalists, who would carry the message further, and the general public as consumers.

  4. My role

    Communication Campaign Manager. I wrote the terms of reference for the campaign, prepared the talking points and key messages, produced the communication materials and press kits, brought the stakeholders on board and monitored media coverage.

  5. Strategic approach

    We agreed the key messages first, then produced materials made for each audience. The campaign opened with a briefing for journalists, so that coverage began before we went to the field, and it was then rolled out region by region, with roughly one major campaign in each of the ten regions. Each region held its own evaluation meeting, followed by an overall review with IITA and IRAD experts and MINADER.

  6. Creative concept

    An invisible danger had to be made visible. The messages were cut down to a few simple ideas a farmer could act on straight away: dry your harvest properly, store it well, and know what mold on grain can do to a family. Picture boxes and posters carried the message for audiences who do not read easily, and the same ideas were relayed in local languages on community radio.

  7. Channels used

    • Field awareness meetings in the ten regions
    • Picture boxes and posters for the field
    • Journalist briefing and press kits
    • Community radio in local languages
    • Press, radio and television coverage

  8. Dissemination approach

    The journalist briefing came first, giving the media the facts and the language to report the issue properly. The field campaigns followed, one region at a time, each one feeding local coverage. Journalists relayed the message in the press, on radio and on television, with community radio broadcasting in local languages so that producers heard it in their own words. I monitored coverage throughout, and each region reviewed its results before the final evaluation.

  9. Measurable results

    30,000 producers were reached in one month, and 200 journalists were trained on the dangers of aflatoxin and equipped to report on them. Coverage included around twenty articles, a dozen reports and some fifty broadcast programmes, many in local languages on community radio. The campaign put the subject on the public agenda and led to two recommendations: an integrated, multisectoral strategy against moulds and aflatoxin, and a high-level symposium under MINADER to prepare it.

Results at a glance

30,000producers reached
200journalists trained
10regions covered in one month
80+articles, reports and broadcasts

Campaign 3

“Decisive match for major achievements”: making Cameroon’s Growth and Employment Strategy understood

A national development strategy explained as a football match, so that people with little formal schooling could see where they stood in it.

Institutions
MINEPAT and PNDP
Country
Cameroon
Period
2011
My title
Communication Campaign Manager and designer of the concept

  1. Communication challenge

    The Growth and Employment Strategy Paper set the country’s course for the 2010–2020 decade under Vision 2035: fighting unemployment, growth of 5.5% a year, modern agriculture, roads, energy and water. After its official launch, and despite earlier awareness work, Cameroonians showed little interest in it and little sense of ownership.

  2. Objectives

    Make the strategy understood and adopted by as many Cameroonians as possible, so that the goals set out in it could actually be reached.

  3. Target audiences

    Young people, the middle class, rural populations, citizens with an average level of formal education, and football supporters, who were very numerous in Cameroon at the time.

  4. My role

    I designed the concept and managed the campaign. I tested the idea, brought together the multidisciplinary team that produced the final version, took it through validation and led its dissemination, up to presenting it to the Presidency of the Republic following a memo requested by the Civil Cabinet.

  5. Strategic approach

    The idea was tried out first at the scale of a single local development project, to see how people reacted. The response was strong enough that international partners, including the French Ambassador and the World Bank Country Director for Cameroon, said as much openly. I then built a multidisciplinary team to produce the final concept, had it validated, and only then moved to wide dissemination.

  6. Creative concept

    Football was the country’s most popular sport, so the strategy was drawn as a decisive match. One team lines up Vision 2035, decentralisation, peace and democracy, jobs, youth and women, the diaspora and the major projects. Facing them stand unemployment, poor infrastructure, bad governance, corruption and underdevelopment. The Cameroonian people are the referee, development partners are friends of Cameroon on the touchline, and the President is the coach. There are no spectators, because everyone has to be on the pitch. The concept also makes an uncomfortable point plainly: an official who embezzles public money may believe he is on the national team, but he is wearing the number 8 shirt of the opposing side. A single image explained a policy document that most people would never read.

  7. Channels used

    • Large-format display at Promote 2011, Palais des Congrès
    • Insert in the national daily Cameroon Tribune
    • 120,000 printed copies
    • Presentation to the Presidency of the Republic
    • Reproduction by other media

  8. Dissemination approach

    The concept was unveiled on a large format at Promote 2011, Cameroon’s biggest international trade fair, where it was seen by close to 20,000 visitors. That reception led to instructions to take it further: 120,000 A4 copies were printed and distributed with Cameroon Tribune, the bilingual state daily, and several media outlets reproduced the concept in their own publications. Two further steps were planned but never took place: adapting the image for the digital billboards then appearing in Yaounde and Douala, and a 3D version for television and the internet.

  9. Measurable results

    More than 120,000 copies were distributed through Cameroon Tribune, around 20,000 visitors saw the concept at Promote 2011, and other media reproduced it, which extended its reach at no cost. No satisfaction survey was carried out, so I make no claim about measured opinion change. What is certain is that the strategy gained visibility and a form of public support through a campaign unlike anything used for it before.

Results at a glance

20,000visitors saw it at Promote 2011
